meta.blurb: Elena makes one small mistake at work, and a cruel voice in her head will not stop. Her aunt invites her to a Thursday circle in the library, where she learns, step by step, how to be on her own side.
meta.bible: Elena Costa: a translator in her thirties who works from home; careful, shy and hard on herself. Rosa Costa: her aunt, who once ran a small flower shop for six years; she leads the Thursday circle; wise, humorous and gentle. Walter: a retired bus driver and churchgoer in the circle. Hana: a young Muslim student in the circle. Dev: a quiet man in the circle. Mr Hartley: Elena's client, who replies kindly. Millbrook Library: where the Thursday circle meets in the back room, with tea and biscuits. Ideas and traditions, each correctly attributed and treated with respect: Metta, loving-kindness, an early Buddhist practice in the Pali language, and an early Buddhist text in which a king finds that no one is dearer to him than himself; Hillel and the Pirkei Avot, a Jewish collection of ethical sayings: if I am not for myself, who will be for me; the Christian and Jewish command to love your neighbour as yourself; the hadith, a saying recorded of the Prophet Muhammad that the body has a right over you; Guilt versus Shame; Perfectionism; Boundaries; Common humanity. Research on self-kindness is described as suggestive and still growing, never as settled. The three questions: what am I feeling, what do I need, what would I say to a friend. Radical comes from the Latin word for root. Beats 41 and 50 say that a doctor, a counsellor or a crisis line is the right help when pain is heavy; this book is general ideas, not treatment. Voice and tone: warm, plain, gently funny, never preachy.

B1B2: Elena Costa is a translator, and she works from a small desk at home. This morning she sent an important contract to a client, and she has just seen a wrong number in it.
At once a voice in her head began to scold her. It said that she was careless, that she was a fraud, and that everyone would soon know.
Later, Elena thought about her best friend, who had once made a mistake at work. She had comforted her kindly, and she would never have used those cruel words.
Elena told her aunt Rosa about the mistake on the phone. Rosa listened carefully and then invited her to a small group that met on Thursdays at the library.
The circle was small and friendly, and everyone sat together in a warm room. Six people held mugs of tea, and Rosa began with one simple question about how everyone was feeling.
Rosa explained that being kind to yourself is not the same as being selfish. It simply means treating your own pain with the care you would give a friend.
Elena worried that being kind to herself would make her lazy. Rosa said that some research suggests the opposite, because people who are gentle with themselves often find it easier to try again.
Rosa read from an old Buddhist text, in which a king searches the whole world in his thoughts. He finds that no one is dearer to him than himself, and so he sees that others feel the same.
Next, Rosa described the Buddhist practice of loving-kindness, or metta. In it you quietly offer good wishes, first to yourself and then to other people.
That night Elena tried some of the traditional phrases at home. She whispered, “May I be safe, may I be well, may I be at ease,” and she felt a little silly.
Rosa suggested placing a hand on her heart in hard moments. The warmth and the gentle pressure of a hand can feel comforting, and many people say it helps them to settle.
Rosa said that the harsh inner voice usually believes it is protecting you. You can thank it for trying, she said, without having to obey it.
Rosa asked everyone to write a letter to themselves as a kind friend would. Elena wrote about the contract, and she was surprised by how gentle her words became.
Hana, a student in the circle, said that her mistakes always made her feel alone. Rosa said that this feeling is almost universal, and that everyone makes mistakes and has hard days.
Walter, an older member of the group, was a churchgoer. He pointed out that the command to love your neighbour as yourself seems to take self-love for granted.
Rosa read a saying from the Jewish tradition, recorded in the Pirkei Avot. It asks, “If I am not for myself, who will be for me?”
Hana, who is Muslim, shared a saying recorded in the hadith collections. It says that your body has a right over you, so rest and food are not selfish.
Guilt, Rosa said, tells us that we did something wrong. Shame is crueller, because it tells us that we are something wrong, and that voice does not help us to change.
Elena asked whether being kind to herself meant ignoring the mistake. Rosa said no, because real kindness includes owning the mistake, apologising and putting it right.
The next morning, Elena wrote a short email to her client. She corrected the number, apologised plainly and attached the new document.
Within an hour, her client Mr Hartley replied to her message. He thanked her for catching the error so quickly and said that such things happen to everyone.
After the stress of the week, Elena felt completely tired. Rosa told her that tiredness makes the harsh voice louder, so she took a long nap.
A colleague asked Elena to take on another job that evening. For the first time she said no, politely, and she realised that boundaries are a form of kindness.
Walter said that he had always tried to be perfect. Rosa told him that high standards are fine, but cruel standards do not help, and that good enough is often really good.
Elena often looked at the happy photos that friends posted online. Rosa said that we usually compare our private worries with other people's best moments.
When sadness comes, Rosa taught her, do not push it away. Instead say quietly that this hurts, and that it makes sense that it hurts.
Rosa gave them three questions to use in hard moments. What am I feeling, what do I need, and what would I say to a friend?
A senior colleague told Elena that her report needed more work. She felt the old shame rise, but she paused, breathed and asked what was true and useful.
In the circle, Elena remembered a school exam that she had failed when she was twelve. She told herself that the girl she had been was frightened and young, and had done her best.
Rosa said that the inner critic often borrows voices from long ago. They may belong to a teacher, a parent or a culture that valued perfect results.
Rosa told the circle about her small flower shop, which closed after six years. For months she had called herself a failure, until a friend asked her to stop.
Rosa said that kindness can be very small and very ordinary. Elena began to drink water, eat proper lunches and spend ten minutes outside every day.
Rosa told them that kindness also means having some fun. That evening, Elena put on her favourite music, and she danced around her living room.
Hana said that she hated her body, and she spoke very quietly. Rosa suggested that she thank her body for what it does, such as walking, hugging and carrying her through every single day.
Elena noticed a change in how she treated other people. As she grew gentler with herself, she became more patient with her colleagues and listened with more care.
Rosa said that the word radical means going to the root. Kindness must be there especially on the days when we fail to be kind.
After a good month, one bad day came along. Elena made a small mistake, and the cruel voice returned at full volume, but this time she noticed it sooner.
Dev, a quiet man in the circle, asked whether kindness meant putting up with everything. Rosa said no, because kindness to yourself also means staying away from people who treat you badly.
Every morning, Elena sat on a cushion for five minutes. She followed her breath and repeated the kind phrases, and her mornings began to feel different.
Rosa explained that loving-kindness can grow outward step by step. Elena tried sending good wishes to a difficult neighbour, and she was surprised that it softened her anger.
Rosa said one more important thing before the group went home. If your pain feels too heavy or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please speak to a doctor, a counsellor or a helpline.
At the end of the month, Elena told her whole story to the circle. When she finished, the others shared their own stories, and the room felt warm.
Her manager asked Elena to lead a large project. She felt afraid, but she accepted it and promised herself that she would make mistakes kindly.
Halfway through the project, Elena found a small mistake in her own work. She breathed out, said a kind word to herself and corrected it in two minutes.
Rosa said that kindness is a practice, like a path across a field. The more you walk it, the easier it becomes to follow.
Elena made her own morning practice, and it had only three steps. She breathed, she put a hand on her heart and she said one kind sentence to herself.
Elena thanked her aunt for starting the Thursday circle. Rosa smiled and said that she had only opened a door, and that Elena had walked through it herself.
Over the autumn, the circle grew from six people to ten. New members arrived, tired and hopeful, and Elena found herself welcoming them with a cup of tea.
At the final meeting, Rosa wrote five lessons on a sheet of paper. Pause, put a hand on your heart, speak kindly, remember that you are not alone, and begin again.
These days, when Elena makes a mistake, she speaks to herself as she would to a friend. If your own pain ever feels too heavy, please talk to a doctor or a counsellor.
C1C2: Elena Costa translated contracts for a living, and her careful work was the thing she was proudest of in the world. This morning she had sent an important document to a client, and a moment later she noticed that one figure on page three was wrong. Her stomach dropped as though the floor of her small flat had quietly vanished beneath her feet.

At once a familiar voice began to speak inside her head, and it was not gentle. It told her that she was careless and stupid, that she had been fooling people for years, and that this mistake would finally prove it. The voice was so fluent and so sure of itself that she had almost stopped noticing it was there.

Later that afternoon, still shaken, Elena remembered the time her closest friend had lost an important file at work. She had comforted her warmly and told her that anyone could make such a mistake, and she would never have dreamed of using the words that now rang in her own ears. It struck her as odd that she gave strangers a patience she refused herself.

When Elena told her aunt Rosa what had happened, the older woman listened without interrupting and then proposed something unexpected. A small group of friends and neighbours met each Thursday evening in the back room of Millbrook Library, she said, to practise being kinder to themselves. Elena, who found the idea slightly embarrassing, heard herself accept before she could think of an excuse.

The Thursday circle turned out to be modest and warm, with six people on mismatched chairs, a plate of biscuits and a large pot of tea. Rosa opened each evening with a single question, asked how everyone was truly feeling, and then let the silence do its quiet work. There was no stage, no expert and no sales pitch, only people willing to be honest.

Rosa began by clearing away a common misunderstanding, which was that kindness toward oneself is a form of selfishness or weakness. It is neither, she said, for it simply means meeting your own pain with the same warmth you would offer anyone you cared about. Nobody in the room argued, though several of them looked as if they had been quietly arguing with the idea for years.

Elena confessed her biggest fear, which was that if she stopped being hard on herself she would stop trying altogether. Rosa answered that some psychological research points the other way, since people who treat their failures with kindness often recover faster and are more willing to try again. The evidence is still growing, she added honestly, but the old belief that cruelty is the best teacher has never been proven.

Rosa then spoke of an early Buddhist text in which a king, searching the whole world in his thoughts, finds that nobody is dearer to him than his own self. The text draws a gentle conclusion, which is that everyone else holds themselves equally dear, and therefore no one should harm another or neglect themselves. The idea, she said, is more than two thousand years old, and it is still waiting for many of us to believe it.

Rosa explained that many Buddhists practise loving-kindness, known in the old Pali language as metta, which means repeating warm wishes for oneself and then for others. Teachers often begin with the person who seems easiest, and for some people that is a pet or a child, while for many it is surprisingly difficult to begin with themselves. The practice is not about forcing a feeling, she said, but about planting a seed.

At home that night Elena sat on her bed and tried the traditional phrases, which vary from teacher to teacher but always sound much the same. She whispered that she might be safe, might be well and might be at ease, and she felt ridiculous, as if she were acting in a play. Rosa had warned her that this awkwardness was normal, and that it usually fades with time.

Rosa had a simple suggestion for the moments when words failed, which was to rest a hand gently on the heart or the cheek. Many people find that the warmth and weight of a caring touch calms the body, even when the touch is their own, though it does not work for everyone. Elena felt faintly foolish for a moment, then noticed that her breathing had slowed.

The inner critic, Rosa said, is rarely a villain, for it usually believes that harsh words will keep us safe from failure and shame. We may therefore thank it for its concern, and then decline, politely and firmly, to take its advice. Elena found that she could imagine her critic as an anxious old guard who had been on duty for far too long.

For the week's exercise Rosa asked each of them to write a letter to themselves in the voice of a wise and loving friend. Elena described the mistake in the contract plainly, and then, to her own surprise, wrote that everyone slips sometimes and that she had always been careful and conscientious. When she read it back, her eyes stung, because she realised she had never spoken to herself that way before.

Hana, a young student in the circle, admitted that after any failure she felt as though she were the only person who ever got things wrong. Rosa answered that this sense of being uniquely flawed is among the most common human feelings, and that nearly everyone in the room, and in the world, carries it in secret. A mistake, she said, is not proof that we are different but a sign that we belong to the human family.

Walter, a retired bus driver who had attended church all his life, observed that the old command to love your neighbour as yourself seems to assume a certain love of the self. Many Christian and Jewish teachers have said much the same, he added, though they argue about how far the idea reaches. Rosa thanked him and said that one need not share his faith to find the phrase worth thinking about.

Rosa then quoted a well-known saying attributed to the Jewish teacher Hillel in the Pirkei Avot, a collection of ethical teachings. He asked, if I am not for myself, who will be for me, and the same passage goes on to ask what a person is if they are only for themselves. Balance, then, was the heart of it, and kindness toward oneself was one side of the scale.

Hana, who was a Muslim, shared a saying that is recorded in the hadith collections and attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, which reminds the believer that the body has a right over them. In her family it was often quoted to people who worked too hard, and it meant that rest, food and care are duties and not indulgences. Elena felt something loosen in her chest as she listened, as if a tight belt had been quietly undone.

Rosa drew a careful line between two feelings that people often mix up, which are guilt and shame. Guilt says that I did something wrong, and it can lead us to apologise and repair the damage, whereas shame says that I am something wrong, and it usually leads only to hiding. Elena realised that her inner voice had been speaking almost entirely in the language of shame.

Elena wondered aloud whether all this kindness might simply be a clever way of avoiding responsibility. Rosa shook her head and said that the opposite was true, because it is far easier to look at a mistake clearly when we are not afraid of being destroyed by it. A kind person can say that she was wrong, and then calmly mend what can be mended.

The following morning Elena wrote to her client, gave the corrected figure, apologised in two plain sentences and attached the revised document. She did not grovel or make excuses, and she noticed that the task was much easier without the voice screaming over her shoulder. When she pressed send, her heart was beating fast but her hands were remarkably steady.

Within the hour a reply came from Mr Hartley, her client, and it was brief and perfectly friendly. He thanked her for spotting the problem so promptly, noted that errors happen in every office, and asked her to send the revised version when it was ready. Elena read the message three times, half expecting to find a hidden reproach, and found only ordinary courtesy.

After three days of anxiety Elena was exhausted, and Rosa pointed out that tiredness makes the inner critic considerably louder. Kindness, she said, is often as practical as a nap, a hot meal or a walk in the fresh air, and none of these things needs to be earned. Elena lay down, slept for two hours, and woke feeling like a different and gentler person.

A colleague asked Elena to take on an extra translation that same evening, and the old reflex to say yes at any cost rose automatically within her. This time she paused, noticed how tired she was and declined politely, offering another day instead. It felt, she told the circle, like closing a window in a draught, and she was surprised that nobody was offended.

The conversation turned to perfectionism, and Walter admitted that he had spent his whole working life trying never to make an error. Rosa said that high standards are a fine thing, but that a standard no human being can meet is simply a method of punishment, and that work which is good enough is usually very good indeed. The group laughed warmly, because everyone in the room recognised the trap he had described.

Late at night Elena would scroll through the cheerful photographs that friends and strangers posted, and each image seemed to prove that everybody else was managing better. Rosa reminded her that we compare our own hidden worries with other people's polished highlights, which is a contest we are guaranteed to lose. Elena decided, quite simply, to spend a good deal less time looking at her phone after dark.

When difficult feelings arrived, Rosa taught her, the first kindness is to stop fighting them and simply acknowledge that they are there. Elena began to say quietly to herself that this hurts, and that it makes sense that it hurts, which was a sentence no one had ever taught her to say. The sadness did not disappear, but it no longer had to be defended against.

For hard moments, Rosa offered the circle three questions that could be kept in a pocket. What am I feeling right now, what do I most need, and what would I say if a dear friend were in my place? Elena wrote them on a small card and propped it against her computer where she could see it every morning.

A senior colleague returned Elena's report covered in critical comments, and the old wave of shame rose at once. She paused, breathed out and put a hand on her heart, and then she read the comments again, separating what was true and useful from what was merely harsh. Most of the points, she saw, were fair and could be fixed in an afternoon.

One evening, in the quiet of the circle, Elena found herself remembering an exam she had failed at the age of twelve, and the shame she had carried ever since. She pictured the girl at the desk, small and frightened and doing her best, and she silently told her that it was all right. It seemed to her that a very old knot, pulled tight for years, had loosened a little.

Rosa suggested that the inner critic often speaks in borrowed voices, which may once have belonged to a strict teacher, an anxious parent or a culture that prized flawless results. Most of those people, she said gently, were doing what they knew and probably did not mean to wound. Recognising where the voice came from made it a little easier for Elena to answer it back.

Rosa told the circle about the small flower shop she had loved and run for six years, until rising rents forced her to close its doors. For months afterward she had called herself a failure in the privacy of her own mind, until an old friend asked whether she would speak to anyone else that way. She had never forgotten the question, and she had been learning to answer it ever since.

Kindness, Rosa insisted, does not have to be grand, and most of it is made of ordinary acts such as drinking water, eating a proper lunch and stepping outside for a few minutes of daylight. Elena began to treat these small acts as quiet messages to herself that she mattered and was worth looking after. Within a fortnight, she noticed that her whole day felt more steady and a good deal less rushed.

Rosa pointed out that kindness is not always serious, and that play, music and laughter belong to the same family of care. Elena, who had not danced in years, put on an old record that night and moved around her tiny living room with abandon. Nobody was watching, and that, she thought, was precisely what made it so delightful.

When the conversation turned to bodies, Hana confessed that she looked in the mirror each morning only to find faults. Rosa proposed an experiment, which was to thank the body for what it does, for carrying us, healing us, hugging the people we love and walking us through every ordinary day. Hana was doubtful, but a week later she reported that the mirror felt slightly less like a courtroom.

As the weeks went by, Elena noticed an unexpected side effect of treating herself more gently. She grew more patient with colleagues, listened with less impatience to their troubles, and was no longer so quick to judge their mistakes. It seemed that kindness, once practised in one direction, did not stay there for long.

The word radical, Rosa reminded them, comes from the Latin for root, and it means going to the foundation rather than staying on the surface. Radical kindness therefore includes the days when we fail to be kind, when the harsh voice wins and we forget everything we have learned. Those are the days, she said, when the practice is most needed, and when it quietly matters most of all.

After a month of progress, a bad day arrived and the harsh voice returned at full volume. Elena made a small error in a date, and within seconds she was calling herself every name she had once used, but this time she noticed what was happening almost at once. She smiled wryly, laid a hand on her heart and began again, which was all that anyone could ask.

Dev, who rarely spoke, asked whether self-kindness meant simply putting up with whatever other people did to you. Rosa answered firmly that it did not, and that caring for yourself includes setting limits and keeping a distance from those who treat you cruelly or carelessly. Compassion, she said, has strong arms as well as a soft heart, and it knows when to close the gate.

Each morning, before she opened her laptop, Elena sat on a cushion for five quiet minutes, following her breath and repeating her kind phrases. Some days her mind wandered constantly and the words felt empty, while on others a small warmth seemed to rise in her chest. Either way, she kept coming back, which Rosa said was the whole of the practice.

Rosa explained that traditional loving-kindness practice widens in circles, moving from oneself to loved ones, then to neutral people, and finally even to those who have caused difficulty. Elena tentatively wished well to the neighbour whose music kept her awake, and found, to her astonishment, that her irritation began to dissolve. It did not make her neighbour's music quieter, but it made her own heart less tight.

Rosa paused before the end of the evening and spoke with a seriousness that none of them had heard before. These practices, she said, are a support and not a substitute for proper help, so anyone who feels hopeless, unsafe or overwhelmed should speak to a doctor, a counsellor or a crisis line without delay. She passed round a leaflet with phone numbers, and nobody was embarrassed to take one.

At the end of the month Elena stood, a little nervously, and told the circle the story of the contract and the voice in her head. When she had finished there was a long silence, and then, one by one, the others shared their own mistakes, fears and quiet shames. It was the most honest room she had ever been in, and it was full of kindness.

Her manager offered Elena the lead on a large and prestigious translation project, and the old fear rose immediately in her chest. She accepted anyway, and quietly promised herself that she would make mistakes, as everyone does, and meet them with patience instead of punishment. The project was long and difficult, but for the first time she did not dread it.

Halfway through the project Elena discovered a small error in a paragraph she had finished weeks before, and she felt the familiar tightening in her stomach. She breathed out, told herself that this was an ordinary part of long work, and corrected it within two minutes. The whole episode, which would once have ruined her week, passed like a cloud over a field.

Kindness, Rosa said, is a practice and not a personality, and it resembles a path across a meadow that is made by many footsteps. The first few times the grass resists, but each walk makes the way clearer, until one day the path is simply there without anyone having noticed it appear. Elena felt that her own path had finally become visible, and that she could walk it even in the dark.

Elena designed a morning practice of her own that took three minutes and required nothing but a quiet corner. She breathed slowly, rested a hand on her heart and spoke one kind sentence, which changed from day to day but always began with the words, it is all right. Small as it was, it set the tone for all of the hours that followed, and she looked forward to it.

Walking through the park on a golden autumn afternoon, Elena thanked her aunt for the invitation that had changed so much. Rosa smiled and said that she had only opened a door, and that it was Elena who had chosen to walk through it, again and again, on difficult mornings. The credit, she insisted, belonged entirely to the person who had done the practising.

By the end of the autumn the Thursday circle had grown from six members to ten, and new faces arrived each week looking tired, hopeful and slightly embarrassed. Elena, who had once been the newest of them all, found that she now poured the tea and told each stranger that they were very welcome. She understood that kindness, once received, longs to be passed on to somebody else.

At the last meeting of the season Rosa wrote five short lessons on a large sheet of paper and pinned it to the wall. Pause when the harsh voice starts, rest a hand on your heart, speak as a good friend would, remember that you are not alone, and mend what you can and begin again. They were simple enough to learn in an evening, she said, and deep enough to take a lifetime.

These days, when Elena makes a mistake, the voice she hears in her head is warm, steady and wise, and it sounds remarkably like her aunt's. She has not become perfect, and she no longer believes that she should be, for she has found something much better in the radical, quiet decision to be on her own side. This book offers general ideas only, so if your pain ever feels too heavy, please speak to a doctor, a counsellor or someone you trust.
